title: McLaren announces latest WEC Hypercar driver for 2027
Ocon dropped - is it the end of his F1 career?
text:
Esteban Ocon's career as a Formula 1 race driver is over - at least for the foreseeable future - after a falling-out with Haas led to the Frenchman being dropped for the rest of this season.

Ocon, 30, was already going to be leaving Haas at the end of the year, with little prospect of finding a seat on the grid next season.

But the acrimonious turn of events in Mexico City last weekend brought that forward by a few races.

Ocon now faces a year on the sidelines, with the aim of finding a berth as a reserve driver, as he seeks to rebuild his career.

This is not the first time he has found himself in this situation.

Ocon was also without a seat in 2019 when he lost his drive at what had been called the Force India team after it was bought by Canadian billionaire Lawrence Stroll, who put his son Lance in Ocon's car.

This, though, feels like it has more potential finality about it. Not least because, 10 years into his career in F1, Ocon is well known within the sport for both his competitive level and his approach.

He's been around the block a few times. His career has not been especially stellar. He has a reputation for falling out with teams and team-mates. And there is a new generation breaking through in F1, led by new world champion Kimi Antonelli.

Ocon dropped by Haas for rest of season after row

Ocon denies reports of physical altercation behind dropping

The catalyst for Ocon's departure from Haas was a falling-out with team principal Ayao Komatsu after Friday practice in Mexico City last weekend.

Exactly what led to him being dropped is unknown. No-one is talking, not even off the record, and lawyers are now involved.

What is known is that Ocon objected over the team radio while in the car to being told by his engineer Laura Mueller that they were switching his run plan from using soft tyres for his race-simulation run to mediums.

Ocon said to Mueller: "No, no. I wanted the soft. Don't do that to me. Come on."

It seems the argument carried on after the session with Komatsu. The announcement that he was dropped for the weekend came on Saturday morning.

Later that day, Ocon put out a statement on social media admitting "a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved" but adding that he "categorically rejected any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature".

That followed a report in France's L'Equipe newspaper saying a meeting between Komatsu and Ocon "ended abruptly, perhaps even physically".

Haas said nothing more over the weekend in Mexico but on Tuesday evening put out what was already being seen as the inevitable announcement that he would not drive for the team again.

Haas had already run out of patience with Ocon long before Mexico City but whatever happened there was serious enough that Komatsu felt the relationship had to end on the spot.

The decline of Ocon's time with Haas has echoes of previous experiences.

Ocon has been beaten by team-mate Oliver Bearman over his two seasons at Haas, just as he was outpaced by Pierre Gasly and before him Fernando Alonso at Alpine, and Daniel Ricciardo before that when the team was known as Renault.

When Haas signed Ocon, his reputation was such that many were surprised they had taken him. Komatsu felt he could make it work.

But the team began to notice a pattern. When Ocon was struggling, he would become defensive and blame the team and car. Tensions would rise and the team felt there was a lack of accountability from the driver.

There were also clashes with his team-mate, for example in Monaco practice when they got in each other's way and Bearman ended up calling Ocon "an idiot" over the radio.

They also crashed into each other towards the end of the British Grand Prix last year.

Competitive tensions between team-mates are common in F1. A driver's team-mate is also their biggest rival - the only person with the same equipment so the only driver against which they can be directly measured.

The parallel need to work together to benefit the team's overall prospects can be an uncomfortable ask in such circumstances.

It's a problem that is causing tension at Ferrari between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, for example, as was also seen in Mexico.

But over the years, Ocon has built an unenviable reputation for both these sides of his character. To outsiders, this can be surprising because he is charm personified with the media, a delight to deal with.

He and Gasly - who were childhood friends before falling out nearly 20 years ago - crashed twice together at Alpine. The end of their two seasons together was the first occasion on which Ocon was released before the end of the season, dropped with one race to go.

Alonso and Ocon also fell out and the Spanish icon did not trouble to hide his distaste for his team-mate's behaviour at times. Ocon also had on-track clashes and team radio disputes with Sergio Perez when at Force India.

Alpine also saw the same pattern as did Haas more recently in terms of self-awareness and accountability.

Alonso put in a starring performance in wet qualifying in Canada in 2022 and stuck his midfield Alpine on the front row alongside Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

That lap was 1.6 seconds faster than Ocon's and team insiders say he simply could not accept that he had been that much slower.

Ocon is said to have insisted there must have been something wrong with his car and continued to do so for several races. The team checked and checked and there was nothing wrong. It was just Alonso doing what great drivers sometimes do and redefining perceptions of what was possible.

All drivers complain. It's part of their make-up. Their motivation comes from believing they can be the best, and finding weaknesses in the car and improving them is their job and how they make themselves and the team more competitive.…

title: Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro review: A modern aero package but it badly needs a change of seatpost
author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
text:
7.3kg(cages, no pedals or computer mount)

SRAM Red, Shimano Dura-Ace, Ultegra

Scope x Atten Artech 6.A+

We first saw the new Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro back in August 2025 for a wind tunnel test when we had a paintless, lacquerless, menacing looking thing that seemed fresh off the factory floor. It was somewhat overshadowed that day by us also having a prototype version of the Factor ONE in the tunnel (yes, we were very smug), but nevertheless it caused enough of a stir at the time and hence to have at least piqued my interest.

Fastforward a year, and in order to review it properly, I took it on an extended trip home to Cornwall to see my family, where I sniffed out some familiar roads to calm my soul on the clifftops, and a few fresh sections to hunt out rare flat roads, where it does tend to shine. It is a fabulous place to ride, but absolutely murderous if you want an easy day out.

Reviewing it as I did straight after hopping off the fabulous Look 795 Blade RS - to be published in the coming days - left it with a tough act to follow, and one it didn’t quite manage to live up to. It certainly isn’t without merit though, and while I don’t necessarily think it’s quite up there with the absolute cream of the best road bikes (or indeed the best aero road bikes ), it is certainly a good bicycle, and may well suit your tastes more than it does mine. Ultimately the front end felt a little languid for my tastes, but more presingly the combination of a slack-ish seat tube angle and a 20mm setback seat post stuck me in what felt like a rather old school position out of step with the modern era.

As always, let's tackle the subjective subject of how the thing looks first; I’m a fan. It manages to toe the line of looking hyper-modern without going absolutely bananas like the Factor ONE, with clear cues from TT bike design. Those hefty, extremely dropped seat stays would be just at home on the brand’s triathlon machines. Ridley also helped everyone out by normalising massive headtubes with the Noah Fast 3.0, something the Nitrogen Pro has up front to go with a relatively wide-set fork that’ll handle 34mm as measured tyres, which is a capacity matched at the back end.

While it can handle a 34 it comes with 30c Vittoria Corsa Pros on Scope Artech 6.A wheels, but not the standard set that I had the pleasure of riding on the Look Blade; these are a collaboration with Scope and Atten, Argon’s in-house componentry brand, and the extremely fast wheels have been reshaped to better suit the 30mm tyres and to better interact with the frameset, all while keeping the Scope hubs and that eye-catching fish scale texture. In reality they feel no different to the standard Artechs, but it is heartening to know they’ve at least been optimised to this machine in particular.

Back up front and you get the same CHB-01 cockpit as is found on the brand’s Anti Matter aero gravel bike that my colleague Tom loved so much. This you can spec when you buy it in either a 36cm or a 38cm width, and with a choice of stem lengths from 80-130mm at no extra charge.

What you cannot do is spec a zero offset seatpost, which is something I believe you should not only to do but also something you do. I’ll go into the why in a sec, but if you do want to do this it’ll cost you a cool £225.

Geometrically I do want to start at the back end. The seat post is pretty set back; 1 full degree slacker than the Look Blade. This is compounded by having a full 20mm setback seatpost, rather than a 13mm on the Look. It is the same as on a Tarmac however, though again with a less severe seatpost setback from Specialized.

Without boring you too much with maths, for my saddle height a 1 degree change in seat tube angle (STA) equates to roughly 13mm of increased saddle setback. Add in the 7mm differential in the seat posts and the Argon puts me a full 20mm further behind the BB; potentially manageable if you run your saddle in the middle of the rails but as someone who has theirs slammed forwards I would have needed a costly swap.

This is all compared to somewhat ‘normal’ geometry bikes. The seat tube angle is 1.5 degrees slacker than a progressive Ridley Noah, and a full three degrees slacker than the Factor ONE, though these are a lot more radical and not everyday machines.

Before I jump two-footed into the aerodynamics, it’s worth remembering the Nitrogen comes in two guises; the Pro, which I have with a lighter, stiffer carbon layup and more pricey build options, and the standard model with lower tier components and carbon, but ultimately the same aerodynamic shape.

With a rider on, at the time of testing it proved to be reasonably fast. Since then, though, we have been fortunate enough to test a load of other new releases, and it isn’t quite as fast as many of them, now sitting around ⅔ of the way down our power rankings of road bikes. While you should obviously read all of our wind tunnel content, and the one pertaining to the test in which the Nitrogen Pro was included, it’s worth bearing in mind that while ‘bottom third’ sounds bad, it is only shipping 7.5 watts to a Cervélo S5 in reality. If you need every watt then this may be of concern to you, but it’s perfectly plausible you could make this up elsewhere, though you could also make up that deficit elsewhere have a faster bike.

It’s easy to perhaps look at ‘bottom third in the wind tunnel rankings’ and conclude that this is a slow bike, but it isn’t really. Seven and a half watts is measurable, though only barely perceptible, and on the flats the Nitrogen Pro feels very much at home once you settle into a decent position, though as with so much of the performance of the machine the thing that seems to be holding it back is mostly down to the position it puts you in.

Having a relatively slack seat tube angle combined with a 20mm setback post means you do feel like you’re hanging off the back of the bike. On the flats, while the bike is certainly aero enough, it lacks that feeling of efficiency that comes with being more over the front of the bike. My hips felt impinged, and more than anything else it just felt quite old school.

On the flat it lacked that feeling of biomechanical efficiency (though it felt aerodynamically so), and on the climbs where your weight is naturally going to be further back I felt I had to spend more time on the tops than in the hoods just because that’s where my weight fell. When out of the saddle, either on climbs or in a sprint, these problems dissipated immediately, but that isn’t a sustainable solution. A shorter stem may have helped a touch, but only in terms of the overall reach and not what’s going on at the hips. Basically it needs a zero offset seatpost, and I think you should factor it into the cost of the machine.

I don’t think I’m alone; I did a basic straw poll (Instagram stalk) of Argon sponsored athletes. Chris Hall, Rasmus Bøgh Wallin, Linus Østdal, and the riders from Team Cranks appear to be on zero setback posts. It isn’t exclusive, and some other athletes weren’t, but from what I can see from a brief search it seems the majority are opting for the option to get them over the front of the bike.

Up front I found the fact my weight was off the back more than I’d like, combined with a slacker head tube angle (0.8º slacker than Tarmac, for example) meant the front end felt a little more languid and slow than I’d like, particularly at slow speeds. Moreover, being over the back means less weight over the front wheel, meaning reduced front end grip. This is, again, solvable with a costly seatpost swap, though only to a point; the head angle ain’t going to change. That being said, if you want a road bike that errs towards stability rather than waspish agility then this could well be a machine for you. On the twisty lanes of Cornwall I often found myself wishing I was on something a little more reactive, but on the flip side if you relish longer, steadier efforts on flat or rolling terrain (once you lock the position in) I think this would be a very decent machine.

At 7.5kg in this spec it’s not a superlight hillclimb machine but there’s a lot of carbon in the frame, forks and in those deep Scope wheels. It doesn’t have the immediacy of acceleration on steeper gradients that you get with bikes around the UCI weight limit (or below), but it’s also not absolutely leaden either. Certainly one more for fast, rolling terrain but if anyone tells me they can’t bear to ride a 7.5kg machine in the mountains I will tell them to go and touch some grass.

Sprints… now we’re talking. That super-compact rear triangle with large, boxy stays in combination with a bottom bracket shell that’s tall enough to sit proud of the outer front chainring just gobble up high wattage efforts and there’s no concerning play in the cockpit at all. I’d have like the tops to sweep forward a little sooner; the right angle transition is quite sharp and can sometimes leave your forearms contacting the bars when you're sprinting in the drops, particularly uphill, but it’s a minor quibble, and not something I cared too much about while bagging a few local, extremely low hanging ego-massaging KOMs.

The Nitrogen Pro, in this spec at least, is a funny old beast from a value perspective and is a little like the Force-equipped Factor Elara I reviewed recently. Everything besides the groupset is top drawer and as you would get on the best-of-the-best model, so you can look at it two ways: either you’re getting basically the performance of a £12,500 bike for £9,500 ($10,499), where a saving of three thousand pounds to Dura-Ace is significant, or you can look at it as £9.5k being a lot for an Ultegra-spec bike. An Ultegra Specialized Tarmac (not the S-Works, which this ‘Pro’ Nitrogen is more akin to) is £3.5k cheaper, but has less fizzy wheels, a separate cockpit, and it doesn’t say S-Works on the downtube.

Personally I actually like this new trend of top tier bikes but with a downrated groupset. Aside from weight, Ultegra is basically indistinguishable from Dura-Ace and Force is essentially the same as Red so it saves a huge wad of cash for a negligible performance hit.

Setback seatpost aside, as this is a problem that I think can be alleviated at a small cost, I think it accounts for itself reasonably well. Extremely fast wheels tuned to the frame and tyres, which themselves are a modern 30c width and not a cheaper option to bring the price down. A decent cockpit, and a stiff package that is pretty aerodynamic in the grand scheme of things, even if it isn’t world beating.

As tested I think there’s a lot to be positive about with the Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro. It’s stiff, an excellent sprinter, and while the handling isn’t lively enough for my liking it is certainly acceptable if you prefer something a little more stable and forgiving rather than hair raising and spicy. I think it’s a bike that, with a change of seatpost that I think is more of a necessity than an option despite the added cost, would be a fine mile munching fast bike for rolling and flat terrain.

I think if you’re looking for something of a do-it-all fast bike then you will perhaps have a better time with something with more of an all-rounder feel.

Looks good. Under the space age looks there isn't a great deal groundbreaking going on however, but neither is there anything crazy and superfluous.

Just a groupset away from top spec. Own brand Scopes are fun, that's for sure.

Perfectly acceptable for a chunky aero bike with big wheels.

The aero is decent in the grand scheme of things, though not world beating, but the geometry has too many implications for me to have truly fallen in love with the thing.

Top tier but with a step down in groupset can be viewed a couple of ways. I think it's a good entry point into superbike performance, but it's not an absolute bargain. Also you have to buy a new seatpost if you want an inline.

title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
text:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections .

Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.

Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery .

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week , has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media , mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.

In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town , which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.

The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

title: Real Madrid close on agreement to sign Manchester United 16-year-old JJ Gabriel
author: Will Unwin and Jamie Jackson
text:
Madrid hope to bring in forward during January

United to consider legal action if they feel rules broken

Real Madrid are closing in on signing JJ Gabriel, though Manchester United will consider legal action if the club believe any rules have been broken.

Madrid have offered the 16-year-old forward a multi-year contract and, subject to final talks, hope to bring him to the club in January. Gabriel is registered with United’s academy until the end of the season and it is understood the club have yet to be contacted by the player’s camp or Madrid regarding the proposed move.

Madrid intend to sign Gabriel via a Fifa loophole that allows clubs in the European Union to tie down young players to professional contracts if they have an EU passport, which Gabriel is eligible to acquire through both his parents.

Fifa would have to sign this off and United are on alert regarding any potential breach of regulations. A compensation fee would be due to United if Gabriel joined Madrid or any other team. Madrid have been approached for comment.

Gabriel walked out on United in September and is believed to be training in Spain. A move to Madrid offers the prospect of progression to senior football via their B team, Castilla, who play in the regionalised Spanish third tier.

Gabriel played in a pre-season friendly for United against Atlético Madrid in Stockholm in August at the age of 15 and had been training with the first team. If he had not informed United of his wish to depart , he would have been in Michael Carrick’s squad for the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat by Brighton on 16 September. Had Gabriel featured, he would have become the youngest player in the club’s history.

Gabriel last season became the youngest winner of United’s academy player of the year award and was the Premier League’s Under-18 player of the season.

title: Liverpool FC owners emerge as potential buyers of Cadillac F1 shares amid TWG uncertainty
Vingegaard’s Dilemma: Chase Another Giro or Risk Everything Against Pogačar?
author: ahood
text:
Will Vingegaard return to the Giro or bet everything on the Tour? (Photo: Getty Images)

The Giro d’Italia just gave Jonas Vingegaard plenty of reasons to return in 2027 with a route that keeps pointing uphill.

A mountain time trial, the Mortirolo and Gavia, and a penultimate showdown on Monte Zoncolan serve up the defending champion a near-perfect course to defend pink as Visma-Lease a Bike maps out his return from a season-ending crash.

The Tour de France ? Some are calling it the Anti-Pogačar Tour , but in many ways, it looks even less inviting for Vingo.

With just three summit finishes and 71km of individual time trialing, the 2027 Tour offers fewer chances for the Dane to turn the screws with his Pogi-killer climbing power that delivered his two yellow jerseys.

So heading into the winter team camps, Visma and Vingegaard face a season-deciding quandary.

Would another run at pink give him a better chance of winning a grand tour in 2027 before another July clash with Tadej Pogačar ?

Or would another Giro take too much out of him and leave him empty in his pursuit of yellow?

The urgent question facing the Visma brain-trust now is how to win another grand tour while also giving Vingegaard his best shot at beating Pogačar.

Vingegaard is being squeezed from all directions as the 2026 season is a wrap.

He’ll be 30 in December, Pogačar remains his bête noire , and a new generation of GC riders is nipping at his heels.

King Pog keeps raising the bar in front of him, and after signing a blockbuster contract extension , he isn’t going anywhere. Behind him, Remco Evenepoel , Isaac del Toro, and Paul Seixas are pumping new hype and ambition into the grand tour conversation.

The Dane who twice beat Pogačar at the Tour now finds himself defending his place as the Slovenian’s most dangerous rival.

Vingegaard boasts four grand tour victories, yet some are already writing him off as the best candidate to crack the Pogačar code.

That’s a strange place to be for someone who ran away with the pink jersey just a few months ago.

And it puts huge pressure on Visma and Vingegaard for the choices they have to make for 2027.

Another pink jersey would underline how good he still is. A third yellow would silence those already writing him off.

So far, neither Vingegaard nor his team is giving much away.

Visma’s official reaction Tuesday to the Giro route offered zero clues. Head of racing Marc Reef praised the course without revealing the team’s plans for 2027.

“To win this Giro d’Italia, you need to have a wide range of qualities. That makes it a really exciting challenge,” Reef said. “We will study the route carefully before putting together the best possible plan.”

This year, Visma and Vingegaard took plenty of heat for attempting the Giro-Tour double.

The first part worked like a charm, with Vingegaard riding away with pink to complete the grand tour sweep.

The Tour went off the rails when he gave up time to Pogačar in the first week and then crashed out on stage 15 with a broken clavicle. He hasn’t raced since.

Team boss Richard Plugge told TV2 after the Tour reveal last month that the yellow jersey remains the central goal for the Killer Bees.

Whether a Giro defense fits into that calculation remains the big question.

Never one to go over the top on social media or give too many interviews, Vingo is leaving everyone guessing about his grand tour plans. No decisions have been announced.

Vingo remains the only rider to beat Pogačar at the Tour, winning in 2022 and 2023. Since then, the Slovenian has been unstoppable with three straight yellow jerseys, but Vingegaard has never given up.

Yet some are already suggesting that he will have a hard time even hitting the Tour podium in 2027 on a course that, on paper, doesn’t favor his strengths.

Ex-pro Michael Rasmussen believes the time trial-heavy, summit-light Tour route reflects the evolving hierarchy inside the elite men’s peloton.

“I don’t think ASO still sees Vingegaard as Pogačar’s main challenger,” Rasmussen said on Viaplay . “I see more potential in the riders coming up behind him.”

Yet fewer summit finishes don’t mean Vingegaard won’t a fighting chance for yellow.

He’s not that bad at time trialing, and the Tour still includes a late showdown on Col du Portet featuring the Tourmalet and 5,400m of climbing. That’s Vingegaard’s happy place.

And who could have guessed Pogačar would have crashed out of the Vuelta a España?

Visma remains one of the most successful teams of the decade, with grand tour victories hard-wired into its DNA. It won’t give up on yellow easily.

The ultimate question for Vingegaard and Visma is what matters more: winning another Giro or going all in for a third yellow jersey?

That could make for a few sleepless nights inside the Visma bus.

There’s another wrinkle: This year’s Giro-Tour bet ended without a clear resolution for the brain-trust inside the Visma bus.

Visma won the opening team time trial in Barcelona, but Vingegaard steadily lost time and then crashed out two weeks later at the foot of the Alps. And even though he was already four minutes-plus behind Pogačar, the team’s data wizards never got the final week of racing to complete their assessment.

Missing from much of this discussion is Vingegaard himself.

The last official team update came on August 17, when Visma confirmed Vingegaard wouldn’t race again this year. Since then, it’s been crickets and his 2027 program remains under wraps.

It’s hard to imagine Vingo not racing the Tour.

He’s Visma’s marquee grand tour leader, and winning the yellow jersey remains the assignment. And King Pog already confirmed where he will be in July.

Would going back to the Giro be read as waving the white flag for July? Some will inevitably see it that way.

But betting everything on the Tour and coming back empty-handed carries its own risk.

Repeating the double in 2027 would come with the same risk and potential reward.…

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’m a little excited that we’re struggling’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
New York hosts the 1-6 Bulls tonight for their second game in a week after beating them last Wednesday.

Chicago is not a team the Knicks should be too worried about, but hey, this is a matchup between sub-.500 teams, so who knows what will happen then and there.

Here’s some of what we heard from the Knicks heading into today’s game.

On a mediocre start to the season:

“Everything can get better… I’m not pissed about the start or upset about the start. There’s a part of me… I’m a little excited that we’re struggling. I want to see if we, right now, can figure it out.

“When you go through the offseason that we went through, everybody celebrates you the way that this lovely city did and the fans of the New York Knicks did, you want to be shaken and brought back to earth right away when the season starts because that grounds you.

“Right now, because we’re not playing our best basketball, we’re seeing some of the challenges that we need to work on. Right now we could be winning games, but it could be false reality.”

On Jalen Brunson’s early-season shooting struggles:

“He’s taking the same shots as in the past. In my opinion, he’s just missing shots. He’s taking the right shots. I think all our guys are, for the most part, taking the right shots. Right now, they’re not going in. And that can be for this reason, that reason, I don’t know, and I’m not going to try to overanalyze it. As long as they keep taking the right shots, keep working on the shots, I think eventually they’re gonna fall sooner than later.”

On the NBA’s best shooters’ slumps:

“It happens. It happens to the best of them because everybody is definitely human and every human has their ups and their downs when it comes to shooting. That’s why we have to keep embracing the little things, because they’re not gonna always fall.”

On Landry Shamet’s natural ability to create opportunities through off-ball movement:

“You could drill it, and guys will pick up on it, but you can tell (Shamet) is a natural with it.”

On the explanation for his unusually poor shooting percentages to start the season:

“Missing shots. I normally make.”

On whether his offseason wrist surgery has affected his shooting:

On Landry Shamet’s ability to create defensive closeouts:

“He creates great closeouts, whether he’s shooting or catching. He has a good knack for it.

“It’s just how he operates. He just finds the right windows, whether it’s benefiting him or someone else.”

On Jordan Clarkson’s role:

“He has a professionalism about it. For a person who is willing to do that — he makes our team better. Great person, great teammate. Off the court, he’s a great dude and someone I enjoy being around.”

On why the Knicks’ defense has been ahead of their offense early in the season:

“We have great coaches. [Brendan O’Connor] and [Darren Erman], they do a great job indicating to us what we need to be doing on the court, and then guys are executing defensively and we’re getting stops. That’s always our goal.

“We don’t think about it. Even when you said that, I didn’t think about it. There’s always room for improvement though, so always striving for better.”

On the Knicks finally increasing their pace:

“We finally played fast. We’ve been playing very slow, very stagnant. We finally got out, we ran.”

On the champion Knicks remaining a work in progress:

“It’s early in the season. I think everything’s a work in progress. Last year, I feel like we probably hit our best stride in the playoffs. So we were a work in progress the whole year. That’s the nature of the NBA season. You gotta keep getting better each and every day, each and every game, and be ready to go.”

On the Knicks’ dissatisfaction with their start to the season:

“I just think we’ve got to win, and I think it’s still early in the season, and I don’t think anybody in this locker room is satisfied with where we’re at. Happy to be in the win column tonight, but, you know, to point to 10 things offensively and defensively that we need to improve on. So the good news is there’s no panic there. Some nights right now, it might be the offense ahead of the defense and vice versa. We’ve had a hard time making shots so far early in the season. Tonight a few went in, but then we had some slippage defensively. So, a little give and take, but luckily that’s not the point. The point is for us to continue to get better and we’ll continue to do that.”

On Mike Brown holding the Knicks accountable and not allowing the Nets win to disguise their problems:

“We have to be real with ourselves. And Mike’s great with that, assesses things in film, calls it as it is. Our group’s great with that. We all understand that by no means — we’re not taking this as any potential fool’s gold. The whole goal right now is to continue to get better, and we want to do that. So that’s the thought process.”

On learning to move without the basketball by playing three-on-three without dribbling as a child:

“I remember growing up playing full-court three-on-three with no dribble, so you just learn how to move without the ball. I’m lucky I had that implemented for me at a young age. I wish more kids and hope more kids would do that moving forward in today’s game. I think it really helps you learn how to play and understand how to move and get open. So, it’s kinda always been something I’ve tried to continue to get better at.”

title: Tadej Pogačar's race-ridden Colnago and Brandon McNulty's rainbow jersey up for grabs in auction raising funds for US cyclists ahead of LA 2028 Olympics
author: Matilda Price
text:
The USA Cycling Foundation's annual auction goes live on Wednesday, with Tadej Pogačar 's race-ridden Colnago, signed rainbow jerseys, and and rides with pros amongst the items up for sale to raise money for American cyclists.

Now in its fifth year, the online auction – which is open to anyone around the world – raises money to support US Olympic and Paralympic cyclists, with the upcoming Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028 making fundraising especially important this year. In the US, Olympic athletes do not receive any government funding.

The first items will go live on Wednesday, November 4 with the auction running through to Monday, November 9, and 99 items up for auction in total.

Topping the list in terms of value and intrigue is undoubtedly Tadej Pogačar's world champion edition Colnago V5Rs which he rode to victory at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2025. Donated by Colnago, the bike is valued at $80,000 and will go live on Friday with a starting bid of $25,000.

There's plenty of other pro memorabilia up for grabs, including signed rainbow jerseys from Brandon McNulty and Ashlin Barry, Tejay Van Garderen's white jersey from the 2012 Tour de France, and more from Demi Vollering, Enric Mas and Kate Courtney.

There are a number of money-can't-buy experiences included in the auction, such as rides with Keegan Swenson, Christopher Blevins and Alexey Vermeulen, plus several bikes, kit, helmets, and gift cards, as well as guaranteed entries to many of the biggest US gravel events, and even an entry to the Étape du Tour in 2027.

Supporters can also bid on plenty of non-cycling items, including sports and concert tickets, holidays and hotel stays, and food and drink.

Starting bids start at as little as a dollar with hopes of raising potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars for US cyclists.

"Our athletes are proof of what private support can do," said Molly Pickall, the USA Cycling Foundation's executive director.

"In Paris, American women won every one of Team USA's Olympic cycling medals. LA28 is the first Summer Games on home soil since 1996, and we want to arrive with the strongest team we've ever fielded. This auction gives every fan, anywhere in the country, a way to be part of the Foundation that supports USA Cycling."

title: The Giro d'Italia's most feared climb – A closer look at the mighty Monte Zoncolan ahead of its return in 2027
author: James Moultrie
text:
A modern icon of the Giro d'Italia will return for the 2027 race after six years out of the action: the Monte Zoncolan. The brute of the Carnic Alps, one of Italy's most fearsome climbs, and on its eighth appearance at the men's Giro, it will serve as the grand finale to the race for the maglia rosa on stage 20 .

It will be approached from the traditional Ovaro side in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, roughly 120km northwest of where the 110th Giro starts in Trieste, offering up an average gradient of 11.9% across the 10.1km to the summit as one of the sport's most savage double-digit beasts.

Even worse than the average gradient, though, is what is hidden underneath the profile on paper – the steepest sections exceed 20%, where even the most elite climbers in the world can be made to look ordinary as they battle to survive, and the suffering barely repents as the road up to 1,750m ticks by.

After an eye-opening 1.65 km at 9.1%, the riders are lulled into a false sense of security as they hit a tiny flat section between Liariis Piazza and Inizia Strada Zoncolan, but they will all know the worst is still to come, and this only brings the climb into the most difficult sector.

The subsequent 4km are raced at a vicious average gradient of 15.3%, and it's here where the steepest pinches will be found, upwards of 22%, and the group will start to thin at a rapid rate as those unable to live with the tempo are forced to fight for cadence and position on the mountain.

With several important mountain days already in the legs, whoever is in pink before Zoncolan will be hoping their gap is all but out of sight by this point, but race organisers RCS have opened the door to late drama as an off day could cause total capitulation.

Anyone could falter on the section after the village in Liariis, but it doesn't get much easier from thereon out, with the next 3km still averaging 13.9% gradient, and the final 2km to the line – where the legs will already be empty and screaming – are taken on at 7.1% and 8.9% respectively.

The riders will traverse through tunnels marking the final kilometre, having almost completed the narrow, often snow-lined in May and exposed roads overlooking the Gorto valley, arriving at the foot via 120km of mostly flat roads, and then two late warm-up ascents up the Passo Duron and Sella Valcalda.

All the way up will be massive crowds roaring on the GC favourites and pushing those in the grupetto to survive the climb, which vies for the top spot when it comes to professional cycling's most difficult ascent alongside the Alto de l'Angliru and Passo del Mortirolo – which, in the 2027 Giro, the riders will have already tackled twice in the same day on stage 16.

Emerging from the tunnels, the strongest competitors will still have a steep final run to the line to contend with, but by this point, it will be clear who is going to add their name to the short list of iconic winners atop the Zoncolan, and it will also be certain on stage 20 that the holder of the pink jersey after its 10.1km is completed will be the champion in Rome a day later.

Lacking the same history as fellow Giro icons such as the Passo dello Stelvio and Blockhaus, the Zoncolan has established itself as a modern icon, with the list of winners in the men's race including Gilberto Simoni (twice, in 2003 and 2007), Ivan Basso (2010), Igor Anton (2011), Michael Rogers (2014), Chris Froome (2018), and most recently Lorenzo Fortunato (2021).

The Zoncolan was first introduced to the Giro on stage 10 of the women's race in 1997, where Fabiana Luperini took victory. A legend of the Giro and the holder of the most titles in what was then called the Giro d'Italia Femminile, Luperini said there was " a lot of fear of a climb like the Zoncolan " and that "To win on a climb like the Monte Zoncolan is a great thing, so I feel proud of my victory there." Victory there propelled her towards the third of her five eventual titles.

Six years later, it made its maiden appearance in the men's race, where Gilberto Simoni conquered the steep slopes en route to his second maglia rosa triumph in '03.

However, on both occasions, the riders started the climb from the less steep and steadier side in Sutrio. It was from this side, too, that the Zoncolan last featured in the Giro in 2021, with Lorenzo Fortunato taking a stunning breakaway win in the fog and cold, as Egan Bernal extended his overall lead.

Bernal's impressive performance saw him break Simoni's record from the Sutrio side by more than a minute, but it's the Ovaro side the Giro peloton will be concerned with in 2027, and it's here that the Italian still holds the record from his 2007 victory.

Four years after its maiden ascent, the organisers introduced the steeper and now more traditional side to the Grand Tour, but it was Simoni who still emerged on top. By this point, he was 35 and sat fourth in GC, but alongside teammate Leonardo Piepoli and Andy Schleck, still had the climbing power to distance maglia rosa Danilo Di Luca on the steepest sections.

Crossing the line alongside his fellow Saunier Duval teammate, Simoni and Piepoli hold the climbing record from Ovaro to Zoncolan to this day at 39:03.

The stage profile for the 2027 race is similar to that from the 2010 edition, when Ivan Basso dropped everyone on the steep slopes and defeated World Champion Cadel Evans in the rainbow bands by more than a minute.

Having started the day 7:43 off the lead, it served as a major gain in Basso's GC fightback against David Arroyo, taking back 3:50. He went on to complete the pursuit of pink four days later as he left Arroyo behind on the Mortirolo alongside teammate Vincenzo Nibali and Michele Scarponi en route to Aprica, where the latter won the stage, but Basso took hold of the maglia rosa.

Returning a year later, the Zoncolan stage was marked by controversy and shortened, with the removal of the brutal Monte Crostis climb being announced to fans' disappointment the night before the race. A replacement climb was inserted up the Tualis, but the race route was eventually diverted to avoid the village where the volunteers protested against the judges’ decision.

The drama didn't stop when the rider finally reached the Zoncolan either. Anton won the stage solo, attacking in the steepest sections, but the most important battle was happening around 30 seconds behind him between Alberto Contador and crowd favourite Vincenzo Nibali.

Contador was booed by the vociferous fans, accusing him of playing a role in the Crostis' removal, and after he waited in Nibali's wheel and eventually dropped him in the final 500 metres, a move which the Italian described as showing " a lack of respect from him ". Neither would end up as the overall winner of the 2011 Giro, though, despite Contador originally triumphing in pink, as he was stripped of his title in February 2012 for doping and Michele Scarponi was named the champion.

When the Zoncolan returned in 2014, the stage was taken by the breakaway instead of the GC favourites, but this didn't mean it was without more controversy.

On paper, it points to Michael Rogers riding away solo from the remnants of the early 20-man move, but he was actually locked into a close battle with Francesco Manuel Bongiorno until the final 3km.

As Rogers took his hands off the bars several times to part the crazed fans in their thousands, it was the Italian rider who actually came undone by the actions of a supporter; a fan in a rainbow jersey's decision to try and push him forward in excitement led to the Bardiani rider unclipping and putting a foot down as Rogers powered away to the win.

By this point on stage 20, Nairo Quintana already had the GC sewn up, comfortably defending his lead up the steep slopes of the Zoncolan. With it, he became the first Colombian to win the Giro d'Italia, and the first South American Grand Tour winner since compatriot Luis Herrera at the 1987 Vuelta.

The most recent ascent up Zoncolan from Ovaro dates back to the 2018 race, when eventual winner Chris Froome attacked away 4.3km from the summit and held off a late charge from maglia rosa Simon Yates in the final few hundred metres.

After a slow start at the Giro, Froome had started the day way down in 12th overall, jumping up seven spots to fifth with his exhibition on Zoncolan. Way down on his best, it looked somewhat like a consolation prize for the four-time Tour de France champion, but his best trick was still to come on the Colle delle Finestre four stages later, where Yates completely capitulated, and Froome's audacious 80km attack saw him move into pink at the last gasp with a second stage win.

In the same season, Annemiek van Vleuten became the first and to date only woman to win a professional race atop Monte Zoncolan starting from the Ovaro side. Taking victory ahead of Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio, the Dutch star claimed the summit with a dominant solo victory en route to the first of her four pink jersey Giro titles.

Who will join the list of winners in 2027, and what drama will come on the brutal steeps of the Monte Zoncolan? That will have to wait until stage 20 in May, but if history is anything to go by, the modern icon of the Giro d'Italia is just awaiting its next chapter.

title: Turned up to 11 – The 2027 Giro d’Italia Women route is tough, but it risks producing a race without crucial jeopardy
author: Owen Rogers
text:
The route of the 2027 Giro d’Italia Women was revealed on Tuesday and presents the peloton with a tough nine days of racing . With four mountain days, including an uphill time trial, and five flatter stages, it will be interesting, but it seems a little like an enhanced version of the 2026 race , won so brilliantly by Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ), with everything turned up to 11.

Since taking over the organisation of the women’s Giro in 2024, RCS, which organises the men’s event, has done a good job in modernising and increasing the visibility of what remains the second biggest race in the women’s calendar. Of course, visibility was helped this year by the date change, which the previous organisation requested, but with the power of RCS behind it, the race has been to places and climbs it would otherwise have been unable to reach.

However, despite that obvious progression, the 2027 race route is not a step forward, just much, much more of the same. The race has been made punishingly difficult, thus reducing the number of riders able to compete for the podium, and it could either be won on the first mountain top finish on stage 4, or we may be faced with a desultory stand-off, riders waiting for the final day.

The 2027 Giro is, in fact, shorter than this year's edition, though not by much. Organisers have slated 1,132km, as opposed to last year’s 1,151, which was reduced from the original distance after the Colle delle Finestre stage was truncated for safety reasons .

However, next year’s race includes a whopping 17,450m of vertical ascent, more than 5,000m more than 2026. And we all know by now that harder is not necessarily more entertaining.

Of course, we don’t yet know whether Vollering will defend her title next year, but she has developed into the most outstanding stage racer of her generation, able to climb better than almost everyone, with the punch to create gaps and the engine to maintain them. With more climbing and the retention of the mountain TT from the 2026 race, the route plays into her hands, reducing, rather than increasing jeopardy.

But it’s not about whether Vollering wins or not; whether the race was harder or easier she would probably still win, such is her class and strength and that of her French team. It’s about entertainment and engagement, getting eyes on the sport and keeping them there, and for that, as in all sports, there needs to be jeopardy.

Jeopardy is why the 2026 Giro was so brilliant. With 40km of the final stage left to ride all three places on the general classification podium were up for grabs until Vollering played her card, eventually winning the GC by 30 seconds with a jaw-dropping ride. I was on my feet from the moment she attacked until she triumphantly crossed the line, awestruck by her performance while simultaneously feeling for Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) as her grasp on the pink jersey slipped away. The day had everything I wanted from sport.

And all that happened on a stage with only 2,100m of vertical ascent, just a bump in comparison to next year’s trio of Alpine stages.

Let’s start with the mountain time trial. It’s the second consecutive edition with such a stage, and last year the TT set up that thrilling final, Van der Breggen’s win startling her rivals as she moved into pink. But such a stage influences the GC hugely, and to include a near facsimile the following year is too much. In a race of only nine stages, to have such a similar defining stage each year lacks imagination.

Like the entire race, this year’s TT is shorter than in 2026, but unlike last year, it’s unrelentingly uphill and will produce some notable time gaps. Better might have been a more sporting time trial, flatter, allowing those specialists who are slightly less capable in the mountains to stay in touch with the overall lead and add some of that crucial jeopardy into the final day.

Don’t get me wrong, of course there is a place for brutal TTs, but we had one last year, so why do it again so soon? Even in a nine-day race there’s also a place for stages with 3,500m climbing, we had one last year, after all, but three in one week? Add in that TT, and we have four stages in the mountains likely to produce sizeable time gaps, especially when two of them are mountain top finishes.

Perversely, those mountain top finishes could be the saving grace, allowing the real lightweight climbers like Petra Stiasny (Human Powered Health) and especially Sarah Gigante (AG Insurance-Soudal), who came close to winning the 2025 race, to challenge. For them descending is the problem and without that to challenge them they could challenge Vollering.

The first of those 3,500m days comes on stage 4 with the final climb to the Passo della Presolana, if that doesn’t decide the final podium, stage 6 will, with even more vertical ascent over two climbs of almost 20km.

The one saving grace about the three Alpine stages is that they get progressively harder, but we really could see the GC all but decided on day four, and if it’s not we could have three days of pure grinding stalemate, the favourites waiting for the final day to make their bid for glory.

On the other hand, RCS has provided some real interest for the five flatter days, even if they do all contribute to the total amount of climbing metres.

Last season the same sprinter won each of the three opening stages, Elisa Balsamo (Lidl-Trek) eventually taking four victories in total. This year there’s less for the fast women, with each of the opening three days covering much more climbing than last year’s corresponding stages, the second stage has as much as 2,100m of climbing, though the run into Genoa is relatively flat before an uphill kick to the line.

Perversely, this could be very good for Balsamo, who deals with punchy climbs brilliantly, but it doesn’t matter who wins, it matters that the race interesting and entertaining, and stages like these invite attacks, uncertainty and miscalculation in the chasing bunch. It doesn’t even matter if they all end up in bunch sprints with the same rider winning, provided there is some of the crucial sporting ingredient: jeopardy.

While it won’t affect the racing, the location of the route also fails to show off what is arguably the most beautiful country in the world. When we first saw the overview map of the nine stages the first thing we noticed was a huge expanse of empty space – where is the race? It seems as though the entire event has been geographically swept into the top left-hand corner.

Of course, nine stages limit where the race can go, and long transfers are hard on riders and race staff alike, but with its diversity and distinct regions, it’s a shame we won’t see more of Italy.

The Giro is always a great race, and since RCS has been in charge it’s far better organised and executed, with better coverage and more fans at the roadside. That is to be applauded, what is not is constantly making races harder but not more interesting, and we should hope for a more even parcours in future years.

title: Could Spain's hardest climb be getting even tougher? Vuelta organisers receive proposal to add gravel sector to Alto de l'Angliru
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
According to a report, a former local mayor has proposed the addition to the Vuelta race director, Javier Guillén, who is set to consider it.

José Antonio Muñiz, the former mayor of Riosa, a municipality local to the 12.4km 9.7% climb, reportedly outlined two options for adding gravel sectors to the Angliru in future.

"The ascent of the Angliru is bordering on extreme difficulty, with large crowds of spectators. We are open to studying its feasibility as long as it increases the interest and spectacle of the stage without overloading the riders or compromising safety. We listen to all ideas, although only some can be put into practice," Guillén said at a ceremony at the climb where La Vuelta Femenina was awarded a gold badge by the 'Association of the Friends of the Angliru', led by Muñiz, this week.

Guillén had previously not been a fan of gravel sectors before the addition of a sector on the final climb of stage 6 at the men's Vuelta this year. The gravel sector was a success, as eventual champion Enric Mas chased down Tadej Pogačar, and Guillén conceded later that gravel will have a place in future editions, too.

Any possible addition of a gravel sector to the climb would come in the first 5km of the ascent, before the road reaches a false flat at Viapará.

The route would then rejoin the usual road for the final 6km and the climb's toughest section, where the gradients reach double digits, including the famous La Cueña les Cabres section, where gradients reach up to 23% in places.

Local newspaper explained the options laid out by Muñiz: "One of the options to include some gravel sections in the ascent to Angliru would be to ascend from the town of Muriellos along a track of about 4km, which combines concrete and dirt, until linking up at the Llagos curve with the traditional climb from Viapará.

"The other option would involve taking the road from Ablaneo to El Cabornín and then ascending a track that would also connect at the Llagos bend, before La Cueña les Cabres.

"Both options combine gravel with concrete on the steepest slopes and would make the legendary Angliru climb even tougher, although they would shorten some of the current 12km from La Vega to the Angliru"

It remains to be seen whether Guillén accepts the proposal for future editions of the men's and women's Vuelta.

title: Manchester United’s wild win against Roma showed angry fans we care, says Dalot
author: David Hytner
text:
Full-back believes 3-2 win can transform season

United were booed off by supporters at half-time

Diogo Dalot believes Manchester United’s comeback against Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday can transform their troubled season and, as importantly, showed unhappy supporters that the players care.

The Glazer family, who have owned United since 2005 and loaded £1.2bn of debt on to the club, continue to be the focus for fan anger and there was yet another protest against them before kick-off at Old Trafford, with thousands of green-and-gold balloons released from the Stretford End. The home crowd sang anti-Glazer songs and threw tennis balls on to the pitch when the clock showed 20 minutes and five seconds, to symbolise the year 2005. The team have seven points from their opening nine games of the Premier League season, their worst start since 1987-88.

The players have also been criticised, with the Stretford End turning on them as they left the pitch after the recent 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth . The fans had previously serenaded the manager, Michael Carrick, who they back to the hilt.

Dalot was the last player to depart that day. He walked off slowly and looked defiant in the face of the jeers. It was a much happier story for him and the team against Roma, with Matheus Cunha’s two late goals sealing a 3-2 victory. United had been booed off at half-time as they trailed 2-0. Bruno Fernandes started the revival when he scored with a retaken penalty.

“These moments are really tough, I’m not going to lie,” Dalot said. “Unfortunately, I’ve had a few moments like this in the past and the only way for us to get out is by winning football games. Nights like this [against Roma] give you an extra confidence that makes you believe you can create these moments – not just for us but for the fans. And it’s important from everyone around the club feeling that we care, that we want to turn this around. I think we showed, especially in the second 45 minutes, that we really want to turn this around.”

Dalot, now into his ninth season as a United player, is a symbol of the club’s difficulties; the muddled thinking. Forced to play out of position at left-back as the only specialist in the position – Luke Shaw – is injured, he has given his all. But with imbalances and weaknesses elsewhere in the defence, the Portuguese’s best efforts have not always been enough. The decision of the United hierarchy not to sign any defensive reinforcements over the summer continues to dumbfound.

Dalot, who has been a target for social media abuse, was a part of the dismal first-half performance against Roma. Carrick took a risk by asking him to push high up the field at the outset, knowing that any turnovers could lead to problems. Which is precisely what happened for the first goal after Kobbie Mainoo lost the ball in central midfield. Roma moved easily into the space that United had vacated at left-back to score through Matias Soulé. Their winning of the penalty for the second goal also came as Dalot was committed forward.

He was asked whether Carrick had told him to play so high. “Yes, obviously,” Dalot replied. “We knew that they were going to play man-to-man but that requires some things that we need to avoid – especially losing balls in the middle because we knew that we’re going to be too open. Obviously, after the second goal, we tried to fix it straight away. I think we balanced a little bit more the game [after that].”

To borrow a phrase from Thomas Tuchel, United played “fuck it football” in the second half. Tuchel said Argentina had adopted this approach against his team in the World Cup semi-final as they trailed 1-0. Argentina scored late goals to win 2-1 .

“If you analyse it really cold, we had nothing more to lose,” the 27-year-old said. “I mean, that’s the unfortunate situation we are in. So we just had to really go at it. In the first five, 10 minutes of the second half, we were winning duels, we were on the front foot. The crowd came with us and pushed us forward.

“Once you create that energy inside the stadium, it’s really tough for the opponents to create even a chance. That’s the biggest thing we need to get out of this game – when we play like this, when you have the right attitude, when the fans really believe that we are there, we can be a very strong team. It is not just the manager, everyone is under pressure. We felt it, obviously. Nights like this can change momentum, they can change seasons.”

United host Aston Villa on Sunday and will need to show the same resilience. “The key message from us [during half-time against Roma] … it’s like we’re getting disappointed too quick,” Dalot said. “Every moment in the game where it doesn’t go the way that we want, it’s like we let ourselves down a little bit. That’s the momentum we need to change.”

title: Real Madrid reach verbal agreement to sign Gabriel
text:
Real Madrid are confident of winning the race to sign Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel.

The 16-year-old is registered to United, but has not been back to the club since walking out in September.

Gabriel, who played against Atletico Madrid on United's pre-season tour, had been expected to become the club's youngest debutant in September's Carabao Cup tie against Brighton.

However, he has opted to look elsewhere for senior football and has been training on his own in Spain.

His availability alerted clubs around Europe, including Barcelona and Paris St-Germain, but Jose Mourinho's Real are considered the clear leading contenders for Gabriel's signature.

Gabriel, who scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, has secured a European Union passport, which is expected to make it easier for him to sign for a club outside England.

United would be due compensation should Gabriel leave, although the figure will be lower if he signs for a club outside the Premier League.

He was named the Premier League's Under-18 player of the season last term, despite being only 14 when the season campaign.

"The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how Gabriel was described by a United source this year, while former interim manager Darren Fletcher said: "The world is his oyster."

Speaking after the EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, United head coach Michael Carrick said: "We've got to be really careful of the whole situation.

"He's a young boy. He's 15 and, for me definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players - their welfare, their well-being, their exposure - we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation."

title: Vincenzo Nibali praises 'innovative' 2027 Giro d'Italia route and says Paul Seixas 'would do well to participate'
author: Matilda Price
text:
Former Giro d'Italia winner Vincenzo Nibali has said that next year's route is one where Tadej Pogačar would be "the clear favourite" but that Paul Seixas is also ready to fight for the pink jersey.

The 2027 Giro route , which was unveiled on Tuesday, packs in the climbing and an uphill time trial on a difficult course that organisers RCS will hope can attract some of the peloton's top GC riders.

Giving his assessment to Nibali – who won the pink jersey twice in 2013 and 2016 – praised the route and the slight changes made for 2027.

"It's a modern Giro, one that continues to innovate while not losing its ties to tradition," he said. "I spoke about it with [new race director] Luca Guercilena, maybe there's no longer a hat-trick of horrible stages, but the difficulties are more evenly distributed, and that's certainly a good thing."

The question of how the race plays out, however, will also be largely down to who decides to race, which we don't know much about just yet, but Nibali thinks the route would be perfect for the sport's biggest stars.

"Pogačar, if he came, would be the clear favorite. I think the route is very suitable for [Jonas] Vingegaard, too. It would be a good challenge for [Remco] Evenepoel," he said.

"And Seixas, after finishing fourth in the Tour on his debut, would do well to participate. I saw him in person at Il Lombardia and he impressed me, I think he's ready to fight for the win. He climbs very quickly and is no slouch in the time trials, far from it... I read that he's interested in coming, and it's no coincidence."

As defending champion, Vingegaard could well opt to return and chase another pink jersey, whilst there are plenty of reasons why Paul Seixas might, surprisingly, opt for the Giro over the Tour next year.

The hope of attracting international stars may be big, but the Giro can also count on a talented crop of home riders to battle for success in the race that no Italian has won since Nibali himself 10 years ago.

"[Giulio] Pellizzari, [Davide] Piganzoli, [Giulio] Ciccone: in a Giro like this, they'll have plenty of room to express themselves," Nibali said. Pellizzari has plenty of time to fix some lapses, Piganzoli is growing rapidly, and Ciccone will find further motivation from the change of team. They need to believe in it."

And in terms of the decisive stages, the monstrous stages 16 and 20 are of course at the top of Nibali's list, but he predicts the race would be open until the very end, such is the balanced design of the route.

"The Valtellina stage [16] is brutal. There's 5,700 metres of elevation gain, so even the thought of climbing it is difficult," he said. "And it's historic, because the Gavia Pass, in the middle of a double Mortirolo, on the toughest side, has never been seen before. A brutal, potentially decisive day.

"And then before the Zoncolan, I wouldn't underestimate the Madonna di Campiglio climb [on stage 18]. In short, you can't make a mistake in the final week. And with the Zoncolan on the penultimate day, the race could remain open until the end. Maybe someone could ride a bit 'conservatively', relatively speaking, and go all out on the Zoncolan."
