title: Hunt 5AM Limitless wheels review: How do the fastest wheels in the wind tunnel fare in the real world?
author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
text:
Hunt has been pushing the boundaries of the best road bike wheels for a while now. I remember kicking about on a set of Limitless wheels a few years ago, before wide road tyres had really taken off, and marvelling at how when I looked down I could see more rim than tyre. Wind on a couple of years and now it has come out with the 5AM Limitless wheelset, with the ‘5’ roughly denoting the depth and the ‘AM’ definitely not standing for ‘Aero Mullet’, but rather ‘Aero Maximised’.

Like it or not, the road mullet trend is here to stay, and this is another new wheelset with a deeper front wheel than rear. Hunt makes some bold claims, but we can park them for a second as the 5AM Limitless Ti-UD Carbon Spoke Disc (to give it its full title) came out as the fastest road bike wheels in our recent wind tunnel test . Wind tunnel numbers can only tell you so much, so I slapped ‘em on a Dura-Ace equipped Look Blade 795 RS, in place of the Scope Artech 6.A wheels it came with (I know, this job is hard and miserable and awful) and gave them a good seeing to.

The short version is they back up on the road what they promised in the tunnel. Well behaved, lithe and responsive, without that nagging feeling of fragility I sort of felt under me with the Scopes.

1,229g (measured) Dark grey £1,999 / $2,599 (£2,489 / $3,199 with ceramic bearings)Shimano, SRAM, Campagnolo F58mm / R55mm 23mmF34.5mm / R30mm

Let’s start with the aesthetics before we move onto the design; these are good looking wheels. Maybe you don’t agree, but you’re not the one writing this review. The vast majority of road and gravel wheels now are matter black hoops with a white logo. Not only are these not black, but a lovely almost steel blue-grey, but they’re gloss. Long have I craved for gloss carbon to make a comeback, because it’s so much easier to live with. Moreover the logos are applied under the lacquer, which makes them look and feel more premium. I always find it incredibly frustrating when the logos start chipping off a set of Scope Artechs relatively swiftly, or even more so how a set of £4k Enve wheels just have vinyl stickers slapped on ‘em; it feels cheap.

The vaguely '80s vibe of the grey continues to the hubs, which also look very smart with the colour matched disc rotor lockrings. I know aesthetics don’t actually make any difference to performance, but I think if we’re all honest with ourselves we all want a set of wheels that .

The rim dimensions are pushing the limits of what a ‘5’ designation can comfortably cover, with a 58mm deep front and a 55mm deep rear. While this is technically road mullet, in practice not even my beady eyes can perceive a 3mm difference in rim depth unless the bike is up against a wall and I’m thinking about it intently.

Width-wise, the front and rear differ slightly, too, with a 34.5mm external width up front for a claimed greater stability in the wind, and a 30mm at the rear, which I assume is also a play to keep the weight down as a system. Both rims have a 23mm internal width, and are hooked. This perhaps isn’t as wide as you’d like if you’re pushing the limits of road tyre widths, but if you’re cutting about on something 28-32mm it’s just right, and I suspect most of you considering buying these probably are.

The system weight is a claimed 1,212g (574g front, 638g rear). On our scales they weighed in at 1,229g, which is certainly acceptably close to the claim. It also makes them 78g lighter than a set of Scope Artech 6.A wheels, which have for some time been a personal benchmark for being both extremely aerodynamic and very lightweight.

Part of this weight saving is down to the low spoke counts; just 15 at the front, with a scant 5 on the non-disc side. At the rear you get a mere 18, with a 2:1 ratio on the driveside vs rotor side. In this guise the spokes are bladed carbon with Ti hardware at the hub end and hidden alloy nipples at the rim for another aero boost. The hubs can be upgraded from steel bearings to ceramic from Ceramicspeed, but come with low contact seals in either case. I tested the steel versions.

I shan’t spoil all the aero details, but if you are a real watt watcher and want to deep dive into just how these wheels performed then I implore you to go and read Josh’s incredibly detailed writeup of our latest wheels wind tunnel test . The short digest for the purposes of the review is that with a 28mm tyre fitted these Hunts were the fastest on test. The margins are small over the competition, but that’s how the data falls.

I’ve ridden a fair few very good wheelsets in my time, and while Hunt has been making fast wheels for some time it hasn’t necessarily had something in the category until now; something to challenge the Scopes of this world. Perhaps this is also because it does such a good job at disseminating its budget friendly wheels about the place that it slightly diminishes its more premium offerings, but here, with the 5AM Limitless, it has a superwheel that’s absolutely up there with the best wheels on the market.

I’m not going to claim I can feel the difference in aerodynamics between these and a set of Artechs; I can’t, and you wouldn’t believe me if said I could anyway, but from a performance standpoint these are the fastest by the tunnel data, and when paired with a bike of the calibre of the Look Blade 795 RS they absolutely flew along. The aero is a given, but they’re so good in so many other ways that I find them so hard to overlook in the ‘best road wheels on the market’ conversation.

First of all they’re hooked. Say what you like about hookless being fine if you do everything right, and I have never had an incident with hookless wheels (because I’ve done everything right) but I’d just rather have hooked road wheels and have one less thing to worry about. They’re also wider internally than the new Roval Rapide CLX III , which my colleague Tom noted made them perhaps a little dated already.

They’re also just about the lightest wheels we tested, besides the CRW Works Ultimo 6060. Weight isn’t everything, but to be the most aero and near as dammit the lightest too is quite something, and out on the road they feel much like the Scopes did when I had them fitted to a Pinarello Dogma F ; fast on the flat, and then this feeling that they just keep being fast on whatever gradient you like.

Flat blasts are a joy, and while they aren’t as stable in the wind as the delightfully placid Reserves that I rode on the Cervélo S5 , they’re extremely well behaved, but they also feel incredible if you like hitting out on punchy climbs. I matched my best ever time up my local test, a 200m all-out sprint at 12% average, maxing out at 17% in places. Close your eyes and you have a shallow, hyper-responsive climbing wheel.

I was a little worried the low spoke count might make them feel a little less stiff. They don’t feel as stiff as a set of Artechs, but this may also be a perception thing as I mostly just felt like I felt less road buzz and chatter through them, which to my eyes is a good thing. They’re more than stiff enough for all-out sprints, and feel great in cornering without being overly jittery.

They’re quiet, too. I have had a set of Hunt hubs in the past that were so loud they made a toddler cry as I rode past. The Scopes are louder even than those, but the Chase SLC hubs here are only moderately loud. If I had my way they’d be silent, but that’s not how ratchets work. The 7.5º engagement angle is sufficient for road, and I never felt like I was caught floating between teeth.

I also am pleased to say I accidentally tested the durability of these wheels. After a Wednesday night hill sprint session, followed by a couple of beers, I went to get some delicious takeaway Szechuan hot pot. So distracted was I by the promise of a warming, savoury, numbing broth (and absolutely nothing to do with the beers on an empty stomach after exercise) that I rode straight into a curb head on. It wasn’t overly fast, but it was hard, and I am pleased to say I neither dropped my soup nor broke the front wheel.

More aero than anything else we tested. Lighter than all but one of the cohorts we tested, with performance on the road that backs up the lab testing numbers, combined with good looks, and all for a price that’s cheaper than the equivalent from Reserve, Parcours, DT Swiss, Roval, Scope, Vision, and Syncros. The only cheaper wheels we tested were Chinese brands, and they didn’t perform all that well in aero terms. Even with the ceramic bearing upgrade they’re still cheaper than most in this performance bracket, so it’s hard to not give them full marks for value.

I am writing this assuming of course that you’re after or indeed . There’s every chance you perhaps budgeted a lot less that £2k and found your mind wandering, and in broad terms the differences are tangible but small to cheaper wheels. While we haven’t directly compared, the wattage gulf will be one that is easily traversed, perhaps a couple of watts in it really, and a small gram penalty too thanks to the law of diminishing returns. Despite this it’s hard to not see these as exceptionally good value wheels given how well they perform against far more premium competition.

I think these might be the best road wheels on the market right now. Maybe Hunt doesn’t have the brand cachet of Reserve, Roval, or Vision, but it’s created a set of wheels that rides fantastically on all terrain, with sensational aero and weight figures that beat the competition in almost all circumstances, and all for a price that’s lower than almost all the mainstream competition too.

My caveat to this is that, for example, if you were building up an S-Works Tarmac SL9, then a set of Rovals will have been designed to work with that frame in a way that may surpass what these are capable of. Likewise the Reserves in the Cervélo S5, but even then the price differential is such that I could look past it, as there’s almost £1,000 between these and a set of Rovals.

Modern width, good looks, good shapes, classy hubs and finishing bits. All good things.

For an aero wheel the weight is maddeningly low.

Segment-topping aero backed up by real-world performance whatever the (paved) terrain.

Tubeless compatibility and setup

I had no issues at all, and they're hooked, which helps the tyre selection worries.

They're still expensive wheels, especially with ceramic bearings, but compared to those from big brands they're a steal for what they're offering

title: 'Tadej Pogačar is more than welcome' says Giro d'Italia director, but Slovenian stages not designed to lure the five-time Tour de France champion
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
The director of the Giro d'Italia has stated the somewhat obvious in saying that Tadej Pogačar would be very welcome at next year’s race, but insisted that the route's incursion into Slovenia is not designed as a bid to tempt the world's best rider onto the start line.

Pogačar has enjoyed taking the opportunity to race on home soil in the past, as evidenced by his two titles at the Tour of Slovenia and his huge disappointment at having to miss this year's European Championships in Ljubljana.

The route for the 2027 Giro d'Italia , unveiled on Tuesday, features two stages on Slovenian soil, with the opening stage crossing the border between the start and finish in Trieste, and the second stager taking place entirely in Slovenia, between Ljubljana and Koper.

This has widely been viewed as an attempt to lure Pogačar to the Giro for only the second time in his career, three years on from his dominant victory in 2024, but this notion was played down by the new Director of Cycling at race organiser RCS Sport, Luca Guercilena.

"Tadej is clearly the man of the moment, so he would be more than welcome at the Giro d'Italia, absolutely," Guercilena said in a video interview published by following the route presentation in Rome.

"The stages in Slovenia are made primarily for the Slovenian fans. Given the proximity of Slovenia to Italy – and specifically to the Friuli Venezia Giulia region – which plays a key role in this Giro, it felt like the right thing to do.

"From a purely cycling perspective, Slovenia is currently producing a great number of champions for our beloved sport, so it felt only fitting to pass through Slovenian territory. If Pogačar were to come, he would certainly be welcome."

'The goal is to attract top-tier riders'

The Giro, by contrast, has 57km against the clock, but 19km of that is in an uphill time trial, while there are seven summit finishes and key climbing tests even before we reach the brutal final week with a monster queen stage 16 and the final act atop the Zoncolan on stage 20.

"I believe this Giro is well-balanced. While the mountain stages are truly significant and demanding, the race’s defining characteristic is the alternation between these tough stages, easier ones, and time trials. This gives all athletes, regardless of their individual strengths, a chance to shine," Guercilena said.

"The goal is to attract top-tier riders, who will surely recognise that an iconic stage like the one to Aprica, featuring two ascents of the Mortirolo and the Gavia, is a gift to the fans, as well as a chance for riders to add a legendary, high-profile stage win to their palmarès."

Pogačar tempted but unlikely to attend

As for whether Pogačar will be attracted, it seems unlikely at this point, even with the Slovenian stages. The five-time Tour de France champion has already indicated his preference for combining the Tour with the Vuelta a España, where he has unfinished business after crashing out while in the lead this year.

A Vuelta title would round out Pogačar’s palmarès as a winner of all three Grand Tours, and would leave more space in the Spring to target the Classics, with Paris-Roubaix similarly the final Monument on his checklist.

"Even though I'd rather ride the Giro, I'll have to tick off the Vuelta at some point too. I think that will be the goal for next year," he said recently .

"I think I still need some time to really analyse what I really want for next year. And I think the final decision will be done in December, where we have another training camp."

'This was definitely the place that I wanted to be' – 21-year-old British rider Tomos Pattinson steps up to WorldTour with EF Education-EasyPost
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
After winning Liège-Bastogne-Liège Juniors and then spending three years of his time in the U23 ranks across two development squads, Tomos Pattinson is now ready to step up to the WorldTour in 2027 with EF Education-EasyPost .

The 21-year-old British rider started out with the Team Visma-Lease a Bike Development team through 2024 and 2025, though he had triggered the interest of EF Education before that point.

“Tomos is a really interesting rider. We looked at him as a junior, but we didn’t have a development team at that point. He signed for another team, and he stood out at all levels, but from what I’ve seen and what I believe, he’s a rider with enormous talent,” said head of scouting Sebastin Langeveld.

“We got in touch again in 2025, and he had a really good meeting. This season, he came back from a small injury, but when he’s going well, he’s a super strong addition for the team. I think we can develop a lot of his skills over the coming years, and he can go long in breaks and be a strong all-rounder who can help the team.

"We’re really pleased to have him on board for the future. We’ve not seen the best of him yet, so it’s a really exciting move for him and the team.”

Pattinson swapped over to EF Education-Aevolo at the start of this season and was quick to jump into the WorldTour team for some races during the year as well, racing Tour de la Provence, Settimana Internazionale Coppi e Bartali and Tour of Austria with the team.

Results while riding with the development team this season also included a sixth at the Visit South Aegean GP, eighth overall at the Circuit des Ardennes and sixth at Coppa Città di San Daniele, his season closing race.

“I’ve had a good season, and I’ve learned a lot from the experiences," said Pattinson in a team statement. "I’ve raced a lot with the WorldTour team throughout the year, so I’ve gained a lot from that and become more mature. I’m happy with my results in races like the Ardennes and in Greece at the start of the year."

The season ahead, however, is one where the rider from Dudley hopes to deliver even more with the aim being to improve in "as many areas as possible".

“Of course, I’m excited. This is a dream, and it’s something that I’ve wanted to do since the start of my U23 career,” said Pattinson.

“I’m looking forward to getting started with EF Education-EasyPost next season. Since I was a kid, I’ve been watching cycling, and being a pro cyclist, being able to call yourself a pro cyclist, is really cool. I like the Cannondale bikes, too. I’ve raced on them when I was a junior, and this was definitely the place that I wanted to be when it came to joining the WorldTour."

title: Our house purchase is at risk from a frozen Revolut account
author: Anna Tims
text:
Access to our £37,000 deposit in a savings account is restricted after a ‘routine security review’

My wife’s Revolut account was frozen in what it calls a “routine security review” over a week ago. Nothing has been requested from her – no documents, the source of funds, or ID – yet, as a result, our house deposit of £37,000 in a joint savings account is also restricted.

We’re approaching the completion of our property purchase and have given notice on our rental home. Direct debits are bouncing and we’re concerned about our credit records.

At one point Revolut also restricted my personal account, so we effectively had no access to any money. We keep being given deadlines for the restrictions to be lifted which are missed, and call centre staff, when we can get through, have little ability to find out what’s happening, or make anything happen. XWF , Oxfordshire

Banks have legal powers, under anti-money-laundering regulations, to freeze accounts if a sudden windfall, overseas payment or unusual activity raises concerns. They are not required to warn customers or explain if they suspect foul play, although customers can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they believe a bank acted unfairly.

There’s no suggestion foul play was suspected in your wife’s case and things progressed swiftly after I got involved. Accounts were reinstated, nearly three weeks after being suspended, and your wife was offered £175 as a goodwill gesture. Revolut says regulatory constraints prevented it explaining. “We’re sorry our review process took longer than usual, and our communication didn’t reach its usual standards, particularly given the inconvenience during an important life moment,” it says.

title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Bulls, November 4, 2026
author: Moritz Wollert
text:
Knicks hope to get back to .500 against the struggling Chicago Bulls

One of the most dreaded speeches a head basketball coach has to make is the one where he talks up an obviously overmatched opponent. He knows the other squad will have plenty of trouble hanging with his ball club even on a good night. On a regular night, his troops would trash the opposition worse than the Globetrotters ever did the Washington Generals. Yet he also knows that complacency can ruin the best game plan and that arrogance has led many teams down the road to hell. Luckily for Mike Brown, he has recent history on his side for his pep talk about the Chicago Bulls.

Those very ballers nearly pulled off the upset against your world champions Knicks last week. Although it came on a second night of a back-to-back and in the not-so-friendly confines of the United Center, the warning should still resonate with the Bockers before they host one of the league’s worst teams. Even if you could argue there isn’t anybody worse than Thiago Splitter’s young group so far this year.

Sitting at the bottom of the league at 1–6, the Bulls have already lost games by 19, 35, and 43 points and sport the worst point differential in the NBA. Yes, even the Sacramento Acuffs have Chicago beat in that regard. While the offense at times actually looks serviceable, the defense has been nothing short of abysmal. They allow 128.8 points per contest, and games against them regularly turn into a shootaround for the opposition. Defending downtown has been especially tough, with teams nailing almost 40 percent of their long-range shots against Chicago. Yes, they’ve faced some stiff competition, but come on.

People in the Windy City are fairly relaxed, though. With a new coach and a young star in the fold, 2026–27 was always going to be a rebuilding year, one they sorely needed after what felt like a decade of drowning in mediocrity. Caleb Wilson, the fourth overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, has been as good as advertised early on and finally gives Chicago fans something to look forward to. The former UNC highflyer is hardly efficient yet, makes plenty of rookie mistakes, and at times doesn’t really know what this basketball thing is that he’s doing out there. But man, does his game look promising.

Wilson is an ultra-modern combo forward with world-class athleticism and a good, determined head on his shoulders. He plays extremely hard, looks to be enjoying himself a ton out there, and seems to possess a drive you usually find only in the cream of the NBA’s crop. If he adds a few pounds and works on his jumper, it’s easy to see the 20-year-old becoming the centerpiece of whatever the Bulls envision for their future.

The same can’t be said for Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis, also two promising young players who have struggled under new head coach Thiago Splitter. Giddey’s scoring has dropped from 17 points per game last season to just nine this year, and he’s shooting south of 37 percent from the field. Rumor has it a wrist injury is hampering the Australian, and it might be a problem all year.

Buzelis’ excuse is that he’s struggled out of the gate before. But even with a world of athletic talent and plenty of promise, he sometimes looks like one of those players who will never really put it all together. It’s still way too early to give up on a 22-year-old as gifted as the former G League Ignite hooper. At some point, though, those gifts have to show up night in and night out on the NBA hardwood, well after the layup line.

Chicago’s most accomplished veteran, Norman Powell, should help in that regard, but how much he can do is debatable. He probably hasn’t even unpacked his suitcase yet, and he’ll most likely be shipped out to a wannabe contender by the trade deadline. Is someone like that really going to change your culture? Powell has played very good ball for years, but can he be the guy who turns things around in Chicago? Your guess is as good as mine.

Even if Powell is exactly the vet presence Bulls ownership envisions, Splitter is still fighting an uphill battle. The roster is extremely young and short on inside brawn (sorry, Stix Smith, Zach Collins, and Nic “I can’t lose to the Knicks” Claxton), reliable outside shooting, and any sort of cohesiveness. The losses should pile up pretty quickly. The Knicks should help their former rivals along and get back to .500 in this one. Anything else would be unacceptable.

But I’m sure Mike Brown will remind his team of that in his pregame speech.

title: Giant Revolt Advanced SL Review: A Gravel Race Bike Perfect for the Modern Era
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
Lightweight frame construction and build options

Progressive geometry, including longer chainstays that promote strong handling characteristics

Increased horizontal stiffness to promote responsiveness and more precise control

A few wonky spec choices, including only a setback seat post

The Giant Revolt Advanced SL is the latest update to the popular Revolt line. The new bike focuses on being a lighter bike with improved geometry, increased stiffness, and refined components. All of these qualities are geared to promote better handling and more speed over rough terrain with large tires.

The bike debuted as a prototype at Unbound 200, snagging a top-five finish in the men’s race. In a race where the rest of the top five was filled with the Specialized Crux 5—the other new release at Unbound—that initial showed the racing chops of the new offering from Giant.

While the Revolt Advanced SL has had quick success at the races, we were curious to see how the pure-bred racer would fare for more varied terrain. On paper, the Revolt was a bike that didn’t have the same compliance and suspension features as other bikes in our gravel bike Field Test . The gravel riding in Squamish would test the limits of what the bike could do away from the race course.

What we found was that the bike was not only fast, but through smart geometry decisions and lightweight, responsive terrain, the Giant Revolt outkicked expectations across even the rougher terrain we took on.

The Revolt has never been the most audacious gravel bike on the market, yet Giant has consistently been a standard bearer each time it gets updated. Even last year, the previous Revolt, already a few years old, stood out as one of the best options in our 2025 gravel bike field test.

This time around, the new and improved Revolt only impressed us more. The high points are things we have seen across the board in new gravel bikes this year: bigger tires, a lighter frame, more aerodynamic shaping. Yet, in a few key ways, it is the details and design beyond the big headlines that are the most exciting aspects of the new Revolt.

That being said, straightaway, the lightweight frame and speed of the bike were the most obvious features. The bike we tested came in as the lightest bike of our test by a big margin. At just 17.3 pounds (7.84 kg), the bike accelerated fast and was able to hold speed well. Giant claims that the bike has a 13.81-watt aerodynamic improvement over the previous Revolt. With the low weight and the aero-shaping, the Revolt felt like a race bike, especially on smooth and uphill terrain.

Adding to that racey feeling was the bike’s stiffness. In a bit of a zag compared to where most gravel bikes are headed, Giant made it a priority to boost the frame’s stiffness. The idea here is that compliance can be found in other components—more on that later—but a rock-solid power platform needs the grounding of a stiff frame and cockpit. The Revolt demonstrates that stiffness during moments of high power, both seated and standing. With tires that take advantage of the bike’s improved clearance, those qualities make the bike such a good climbing option.

The ability of the Revolt as a climbing bike seems obvious, even on paper. What was more surprising was how well the Revolt was able to handle descending and rougher terrain, even with a stiff, fully rigid setup.

After a few miles to get used to the bike, I felt a ton of stability on a wide variety of terrain. At speed, I felt a ton of responsiveness, but not twitchy. It was easy to place the bike, yet unlike other shorter, steeper bikes, the bike was super balanced and tracked well around corners. The length of the rear end, especially, prevents the bike from understeering.

Understeering, which happens when the rear wheel tracks tighter than the front wheel, is a common attribute of many new bikes with slack front ends and short chainstays. I have found it increasingly frustrating since it really holds certain bikes back from getting the most out of bigger tires. With 430+ chainstays, the Revolt handles bigger tires in a much more predictable way, which in turn manages traction better through both the front and rear tires.

All of this added together makes for a lightweight gravel race bike, with solid do-it-all capability, that is simply a joy to ride across the full spectrum of what gravel riding is known for.

The main aspect that I found frustrating about the Revolt is the proprietary seat post. Instead of a standard round post, the bike comes standard with a sweeping set-back D-shaped seat post. While the post does allow for a bit of compliance in the rear of the bike, it does create a bit of positional inflexibility.

That said, the bike does have a fairly steep seat tube angle to counteract that setback. Additionally, the Revolt does lower the stack and extend the reach of the previous versions of the frame. Yet, unlike other new releases, the Revolt has kept the reach of the bike at just 401mm for the medium-large frame we tested.

While Giant claims the seat post adds some compliance to the rear of the bike, overall, I was left wanting more compliance. The stiffness of the bike and the bars feels great at times, but over bumpier terrain the bike is less forgiving than I would like it to be. Bigger tires can certainly make up a lot of the difference, but pairing all of those stiff features with the very stiff Cadex wheels that come stock, and the stiffness adds up.

That said, it does give the bike a bit more upside as a do-it-all jack of all trades.

Lastly, while Giant argues that the bike’s components are updated to modern standards, I found that certain specs like crank length and bar width weren’t up to the standards of 2026. The 172.5mm cranks on our test bike were the longest in the Field Test, and I don’t think they reflect what most riders prefer to use.…

title: A Shimano Shoe Disaster, Bra Doping, and the 5 Biggest Controversies and Catastrophes of 2026
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Wout van Aert’s emotional victory at Paris-Roubaix. Demi Vollering’s rout of road worlds. Tadej Pogačar’s crash ‘n’ comeback conquest of Milan-San Remo.

The 2026 cycling season was loaded with races for the ages.

It was sprinkled with plenty of controversies, catastrophes, and meme-worthy WTFs, too.

Remember Mathieu van der Poel’s pedal fiasco at Paris-Roubaix?

Or the beef-to-end-all-beefs between Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney at the Tour de France Femmes?

And there’s surely no forgetting Jonas Vingegaard’s dungaree-inspired solution to keeping toasty at Paris-Nice.

We’ve rewound through the bike-racing bloopers of 2026 to select the wildest, wackiest moments of the season. Strap in for a recap of mechanical meltdowns, dubious maneuvers, and some debate about “bra doping.”

One of the most hotly debated, sensationally divisive moments of this cycling season occurred away from the damning proof of TV cameras.

The Tour de France Femmes exploded into the biggest beef in recent memory when something happened between Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Demi Vollering’s superdomestique Célia Gery on stage 8 of the race.

Riding at the front of the pack, Gery, Vollering, and Niewiadoma blasted into a tight left-hand corner at the entrance to a decisive kicker climb.

Broadcast footage cuts from an overhead drone shot as the bunch dives under tree cover, and returns to a front-on moto camera shot a split second later.

The race tilted on its head in that one unseen moment.

According to Niewiadoma, Gery took her out of Vollering’s wheels as the Dutchwoman attacked. Niewiadoma was unable to respond and was blown out of the yellow jersey by the end of the stage.

“Gery on purpose just blocked me to the barriers where I had to stop pedaling,” Niewiadoma claimed.

“If they want to compete, they should compete fair play and not look for me to close me in the barriers,” Niewiadoma said. “I feel like it’s so childish.”

UCI commissaires had nothing to say. The cycling world was left attempting to piece together fragmented fan footage to figure it out.

Social media duly blew up with speculation and armchair sleuthing.

Gery was blasted by online death threats.

The final stage of the Femmes played out in the shadow of a volatile, bubbling beef between eternal rivals Niewiadoma and Vollering.

The two superstar riders attempted to turn down the volume on the controversy ahead of Vollering’s crowning stage 9 victory, but by then it was too late.

“Kasia Corner” had launched the Femmes beyond cycling media and onto the world stage.

Alpecin-Premier Tech showed the peloton how not to win Paris-Roubaix with smart tech choices this year.

Mathieu van der Poel and Jasper Philipsen threw away their podium chances in a meme-worthy cleat kerfuffle on the kingmaker cobbles of the Trouée d’Arenberg.

When three-time Roubaix champion MVDP punctured on the notorious stones, Philipsen selflessly handed his wingman his bike.

Philipsen was riding a prototype of Shimano’s new cleat-pedal system. Van der Poel and the rest of the team were rocking the standard-issue, outgoing set-up.

The two aren’t compatible , as MVDP was about to find out.

Clearly unaware of the mismatch, Van der Poel hopped onto Philipsen’s bike and optimistically pushed off onto the cobbles. After a few foiled attempts to clip in, the cobblestone crusher tossed aside the useless bike and walked forlornly back down the verge in hope of some help.

Meanwhile, Alpecin-Premier Tech’s Tibor del Grosso had been busy swapping an inflated wheel from his bike to Van der Poel’s original, discarded ride.

More than two minutes after his puncture, Van der Poel was back on a bike with two inflated tires, a pedal system that suited his cleats, and was chasing hard.

Any hope of a comeback didn’t last long. A few hundred meters later, Van der Poel flatted again.

Team boss Christoph Roodhooft stepped up after the race to cop the blame.

“Of course, that came together at an incredibly bad time. I never thought it would happen,” Roodhooft told Sporza . “We made the decision to use the pedals in race conditions.

“I never thought it would come together like this,” he said. “It is what it is. It won’t happen again, but it’s over now.”

Philipsen dutifully praised his team sponsor’s new shoes on Instagram when they officially launched this September.

“Finally, I can show you what I’ve been racing on all season. The new S-Phyre RC910 shoes and Dura-Ace PD-R9300 pedals,” Philipsen wrote alongside a Shimano promo reel.

“I’m proud to have played a part in their development.”

We wonder what Van der Poel thinks of them.

The only way to beat Demi Vollering in 2026 was to pray she took a wrong turn.

Vollering’s Hall of Fame season suffered its only blip this March when she and a whole horde of favorites took a wrong turn in the high-stakes denouement of Strade Bianche.

An attack group was around one minute up the road.

Only 33km remained to the iconic finale on the Piazza del Campo.

Vollering, Lotte Kopecky, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Anna van der Breggen were in a small chase group with no time to lose.

Unfortunately, they all lost a lot of time when they mistakenly followed a race moto off course down a side track strewn with rocky boulders.

Vollering and Co. rattled down the stony path for a few hundred meters before realizing this was a level of sterrato far too extreme for Tuscany’s white-roads classic.

They pulled to a halt, awkwardly unclipped, waddled their bikes around a full 180, and returned to the race course. But by then, there was no coming back. They were three minutes behind the leaders and without hope.

Who was to blame for the off-course chaos? The moto or the riders?

The driver no doubt made a mistake, but riders are required to know the course.

Kopecky later admitted herd mentality prevailed in the heat of the chase.…

title: Fernandes critical of media 'lies' about Carrick relationship
text:
Bruno Fernandes says Manchester United's players "don't need to save anyone's job" after their improbable comeback win against Roma in the Champions League.

The Red Devils produced a remarkable second-half fightback to come from 2-0 down to win 3-2 and end a run of nine games without a victory.

Fernandes was speaking to the media for the first time since being dropped to the bench after publicly criticising manager Michael Carrick's tactics in the wake of their 4-1 loss at Como.

But when asked if the result would save his job, United captain Fernandes told Amazon Prime: "We don't need to save anyone's job."

He continued: "The club needed that win, the players needed that win. We have been working so hard to get out of this situation all together.

"It's been tough, there's been a lot of speculation in the media. A lot of lies around many things that have happened between me and the manager, that we have cleared the air, then after that the manager took the decision to put me on the bench because I'm not performing.

"Everyone thought that was a punishment for the words that I had. If it was, it was right. The manager is the one who makes the decisions.

"It doesn't change the belief I have of the manager and the staff and every player in this club. It doesn't change my aim to win every game that I have ahead of me."

title: A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?
text:
We cannot know how important Bryan Cristante's foot touching the Roma penalty area as Bruno Fernandes took his initial spot-kick at Old Trafford will prove to be for Michael Carrick.

In the moment, as the Roma fans celebrated, and Manchester United trailed 2-0, it seemed catastrophic for the club and terminal for Carrick's position as head coach.

But the video assistant referee (VAR) Carlos del Cerro Grande stepped in, advised a retake was required - and at the very least changed the course of the night.

Fernandes kept his nerve to drive home his second attempt and then, in a frenzied atmosphere, Matheus Cunha scored twice in the final seven minutes. Even without the context of everything that came before the game, it was the most improbable of comebacks.

Even Cunha's sending off soon after, which ensured a nervy ending, would not deny United a first win in 10, bringing some respite after a dreadful few weeks.

How did Carrick feel when the penalty was saved? And what did he say at half-time in response to a desperate first-half display that brought condemnation from legendary United figures Wayne Rooney and Nicky Butt, who were covering the game for Amazon Prime?

In that moment, there was even a sense of deja vu.

"I knew at half-time against Watford," recalled Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in September 2023 of his own dismissal as United boss a couple of years earlier. "At half-time, I told the players it was probably going to be the last time we worked together."

United were two goals down at Vicarage Road at half-time that day. Carrick was on the bench as one of Solskjaer's coaches. They went on to lose 4-1.

We don't need to save anyone's job, says Man Utd captain Fernandes

Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

Despite the bleakness of the situation, Carrick clearly has a more positive mindset.

"At half-time, I was wanting them to be more positive if anything, and not get too disappointed and frustrated," said Carrick.

"The easiest thing is when you keep trying to do something is feeling sorry for yourself. If something goes wrong, you get disappointed. That's not going to help anybody. We might as well all go home if that's the case. We've got to keep looking for the next moment, the next solution.

"I don't like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do and the history and what's gone before too much, but it's there.

"This place does magical things, it's done it before and it'll do it over and over again at some point in the future. There's just something in this place that when we do have these types of nights, we do it the hard way.

"But one moment can flip the whole place in a different direction. I spoke about that with the boys. Let's have one moment that can trigger it. And we had that."

Rooney, who was almost pleading with United's players to "show some passion and desire" after a "nothing" first half, could only praise Carrick at the end.

"I think Michael Carrick deserves a lot of credit," said Rooney, "because if you were in his shoes you are thinking how can I change this around?

"Whatever he said to the team at half-time, that got them on the front foot and got that belief in them that they could win the game."

Carrick refused to be downcast - even when Fernandes missed that first penalty.

"I didn't chuckle, I didn't smile, I wasn't happy about it," he said. "But it felt almost like 'there's another moment'.

"But at the same time, I was quite calm because I had a feeling the boys were in a place leaving the changing room that they felt something could happen.

"I have to say, for Bruno to double take that penalty - to have the mentality and finish like that - he deserves a lot of credit."

While United's victory was certainly well received, it will not mask wider issues.

'Green and gold' protests against the ownership took place before kick-off and during a first-half when the home side were abysmal.

Chants against the Glazer family, minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and director of football Jason Wilcox will not stop just because of this victory, no matter how thrilling.

The sober assessment should also recall United came from behind to beat Atalanta 3-2 at Old Trafford during Solskjaer's time. They lost 5-0 at home to Liverpool four days later. Within a month, the Norwegian had been sacked.

In October 2018, Jose Mourinho was on the brink of dismissal before a Premier League encounter with Newcastle. United trailed 2-0 after 10 minutes but fought back to win. Mourinho lasted 13 more games.

No-one can know how much time Carrick has bought himself with this victory.

"I don't have a crystal ball to know what happens next," he told Amazon Prime. "We move on to the weekend. We've got a really important game here against Aston Villa, which we need to prepare for."

Chief executive Omar Berrada and Wilcox certainly looked much happier at the final whistle than they had done midway through the first half.

Suddenly United look like they can qualify for the next phase of the Champions League. For the first time since September, Carrick's players are enjoying the winning feeling.

But it will mean little unless they can maintain the momentum against Villa, who were getting beaten heavily by Barcelona as Old Trafford was in tumult.

Asked if he will sleep better thanks to the win, Carrick was honest enough to admit that would not be the case.

"Genuinely, no. I don't. Really, I don't," he said. "Whether that's right or wrong, or normal or not, I don't know, but I didn't feel relief. It was more I was genuinely pleased for the players.

"I know how much they care, I know what they're giving. Sometimes it looks like that, sometimes it doesn't, sometimes we play well, sometimes we haven't, and I understand that.…

title: Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'
text:
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.

In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.

The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.

It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.

The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.

"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."

The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.

Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.

Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.

"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.

Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.

The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
text:
Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.

Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.

A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.

Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.

"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.

AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.

"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.

Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.

CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.

"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.

Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer , external , it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.

Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.

"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."

His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.

"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.

There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.

But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?

Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.

"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".

"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."

Claire Reed, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.

"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reed.…
